Speaker notes

The evidence layer

Archive // method // claims // limits

Primary material

  • Original messages dated 12 March and 5 April 2026.
  • The preserved four-prompt image sequence.
  • A wider Mount Media working archive of roughly 30–40 portraits.
  • Lived experience across Bergen Pride, FRI Vestland, Surviving SOGICE, Queer Fashion of Scandinavia, queer platform research and social media marketing.

Method

  • Situated autoethnographic case study: experience is evidence, with the position declared.
  • Prompt–output comparison: record the supplied image, the instruction, the returned image and the unrequested change.
  • Visual feature coding: compare face, hair, posture and expression across contexts.
  • Contextual reading: read the outputs alongside queer activism, platform research and everyday social classification.
  • Corroboration: cross-read this case against published studies of dataset and generation bias.

What can be claimed

  • This sequence documents bodily drift alongside changing semantic context.
  • An explicit correction — “No beard” — was contradicted in the returned image.
  • The case shows a system automating a familiar social demand for recognisable gender.
  • The output can be analysed without treating the model as a conscious antagonist.
  • An earlier framing that invoked “not male anatomy” was identified and corrected: the claim rests on female masculinity needing no anatomical justification.

Limits and ethics

  • This is one situated case, not a claim about every model or every lesbian.
  • The commercial model’s internal process is unavailable.
  • Masculinity does not belong to men; trans and nonbinary identities are not errors.
  • The ethical problem is classification overriding a person’s own description of herself.
  • Any reading of why the beard appeared is my analysis of a repeated result, not a mechanism the model’s makers have published.
  • OpenAI has not published the training image and caption set, how many queer or masculine-presenting people it contains, how they are labelled, or whether masculine women are labelled as men.
Conceptual anchors
Judith Butler, Gender Trouble (1990) · Jack Halberstam, Female Masculinity (1998) · John Cheney-Lippold, We Are Data (2017) · Jill Walker Rettberg, Machine Vision (2023) · Os Keyes, “The Misgendering Machines” (2018) · Bianchi et al., “Easily Accessible Text-to-Image Generation Amplifies Demographic Stereotypes at Large Scale” (FAccT 2023).

These texts frame the interpretation. The archived prompts and outputs are the evidence for this case.
